title: Things around you and who they belong to
title_target: 这是什么 — Zhè shì shénme
goal: Point at things and name them, show possession with 的, say you have or don't have something with 有 and 没有, and use measure words — something English only does with a few nouns, but Mandarin requires every time.
bekal: use 这 and 那 with the right measure word
show possession with 的 and know when 的 can be dropped
tell 有 (have) apart from 是 (be)
say you don't have something with 没有, not 不有

dialogs.title: 对话 1 — At the desk
dialogs.intro: Andi has just walked into the staff room and sees the things on Wang Li's desk. Notice that every time there is a number or 这/那, a small word appears before the noun.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.id: What's this?

lines.speaker: 王丽:
lines.text: [这是|Zhè shì][我的|wǒ de][词典|cídiǎn]。[中文|Zhōngwén][词典|cídiǎn]。
lines.id: This is my dictionary. A Chinese dictionary.
lines.literal: this — is — I — 's — dictionary. Chinese — dictionary.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.text: [那|Nà][本|běn][书|shū][也是|yě shì][你的|nǐ de][吗|ma]？
lines.id: Is that book yours too?

lines.speaker: 王丽:
lines.id: No, that's Li Ming's.
lines.literal: not — is, that — is — Li Ming — 's.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.id: Do you have a pen?

lines.speaker: 王丽:
lines.id: Yes. I have two pens. Here you go.
lines.literal: have. I — have — two — (measure) — pen. give — you.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.id: Thanks. Do you have any paper?

lines.speaker: 王丽:
lines.text: [对不起|Duìbuqǐ]，[我|wǒ][没有|méiyǒu][纸|zhǐ]。[李明|Lǐ Míng][有|yǒu]。
lines.id: Sorry, I don't have any paper. Li Ming does.
lines.literal: sorry, I — not-have — paper. Li Ming — has.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.id: Which one is his desk?

lines.speaker: 王丽:
lines.id: That one. The one next to the window.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.id: OK, thanks!

notes: **⚠️ A number can never attach directly to a noun.** 两笔 is wrong; the right form is [两支笔|liǎng zhī bǐ] — “two **sticks of** pen”. That little word in the middle is called a **measure word**, and Mandarin requires it every time. English does this with some nouns (*two **slices of** bread*, *two **sheets of** paper*); Mandarin does it with all of them.

**⚠️ [两|liǎng], not [二|èr], before a measure word.** [两支笔|liǎng zhī bǐ], [两个人|liǎng ge rén], [两本书|liǎng běn shū]. 二 is for counting (一、二、三), house numbers, phone numbers, and digits inside larger numbers like [十二|shí'èr] or [二十|èrshí].
**[的|de] shows possession,** like English *'s*. [我的书|wǒ de shū] = my book. If what's owned is already clear, the noun can be dropped and 的 stands alone: [那是李明的|Nà shì Lǐ Míng de] = that's Li Ming's.
**⚠️ The negative of 有 is 没有, not 不有.** It's the only verb in Mandarin that can never be negated with 不. Learn it as one unit: [没有|méiyǒu]. In fast speech it's often shortened to just [没|méi].
**[给你|Gěi nǐ] = “here you go”** — said while handing something over. Very common; far more natural than a long sentence.
**[好的|Hǎo de] = “OK, sure”.** A short way to agree, slightly softer than just [好|hǎo].

grammars.title: 这 / 那 / 哪 + measure word + noun
body: This is a frame you'll use every day. Notice that **the measure word can't be skipped**, even when there's no number at all.

head: Measure word
Used for
Example
rows: [一个人|yí ge rén], [两个问题|liǎng ge wèntí]
Flat things: paper, tables, tickets, photos
Small long things: pens, pencils, cigarettes
Things with a handle: chairs, umbrellas, knives, keys

after: If you truly forget the right measure word, **use 个**. It sounds a bit childish, but it's fully understood — and far better than stopping mid-sentence. The full list is in the appendix at the back of this course.

grammars.title: 的 — the possessive marker, and when to drop it
body: The structure: **owner + 的 + thing owned** — the same order as English *'s*: [我的书|wǒ de shū] = my book, [老师的书|lǎoshī de shū] = the teacher's book.

head: Example
Meaning
Is 的 required?
rows: **Can be dropped** — an institution you belong to
的 stands alone; the thing is already clear

after: Rule of thumb: **when the relationship is part of who someone is** — family, friends, school, office, country — 的 is often dropped, and it actually sounds warmer. For objects, 的 is almost always used.
⚠️ Don't confuse it with 得 and 地, which are also read *de*. The three have different jobs; only **的** is used for possession.

grammars.title: 有 and 没有 — have, there is

head: Form
Example
Meaning
rows: [我有一个哥哥|Wǒ yǒu yí ge gēge]。

after: ⚠️ **Don't mix up 有 and 是.** 是 links two things that are **the same** (“this is a dictionary”). 有 means **to have** or **there is** (“I have a dictionary”). [这是词典|Zhè shì cídiǎn] ≠ [我有词典|Wǒ yǒu cídiǎn].
有 also means “there is” for saying something exists somewhere — [桌子上有一本书|Zhuōzi shang yǒu yì běn shū] “there's a book on the table”. This is covered fully in Unit 6.

dialogs.title: 对话 2 — Left behind
dialogs.intro: After class, Li Ming is looking for something. Notice how 的 is used with no noun after it.

lines.speaker: 李明:
lines.text: [安迪|Āndí]，[你|nǐ][看见|kànjiàn][我的|wǒ de][手机|shǒujī][了|le][吗|ma]？
lines.id: Andi, have you seen my phone?

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.text: [没有|Méiyǒu]。[你的|Nǐ de][手机|shǒujī][是|shì][什么|shénme][颜色|yánsè][的|de]？
lines.id: No. What color is your phone?
lines.literal: not-have. you — 's — phone — is — what — color — (one).

lines.speaker: 李明:
lines.id: A black one. That old one.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.text: [桌子上|Zhuōzi shang][有|yǒu][一|yí][个|ge][黑色|hēisè][的|de][手机|shǒujī]。[是|Shì][你的|nǐ de][吗|ma]？
lines.id: There's a black phone on the desk. Is it yours?
lines.literal: desk — on — there-is — one — (measure) — black — (de) — phone. is — you — 's — (question).

lines.speaker: 李明:
lines.id: Which desk?

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.id: The one next to the door.

lines.speaker: 李明:
lines.text: [啊|A]，[是|shì][我的|wǒ de]！[太好了|Tài hǎo le]！[谢谢|Xièxie]！
lines.id: Ah, it's mine! What a relief! Thank you!
lines.literal: ah, is — I — 's. too — good — (change). thanks.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.text: [不客气|Bú kèqi]。[你|Nǐ][还|hái][有|yǒu][别的|bié de][东西|dōngxi][吗|ma]？
lines.id: You're welcome. Anything else?
lines.literal: not — polite. you — still — have — other — (de) — thing — (question).

lines.speaker: 李明:
lines.id: No, that's it. Everything's here.

notes: **[什么颜色的|shénme yánsè de]？** — “what color one?”. The 的 at the end stands in for a noun that's already clear. The answer uses 的 too: [黑色的|Hēisè de] = a black one.
**Adjective + 的 + noun.** [很旧的手机|hěn jiù de shǒujī] = an old phone. When the adjective is a single syllable, 的 is often dropped: [新手机|xīn shǒujī] new phone, [旧书|jiù shū] used book.

**⚠️ Descriptions always come BEFORE the thing they describe.** English says “the desk **next to the door**”; Mandarin says [门旁边的那张桌子|mén pángbiān de nà zhāng zhuōzi] — “door beside 's that desk”. This is the reverse of English and takes a few days to feel natural.
**[没有了|Méiyǒu le] = “there's nothing left”.** The 了 at the end marks a **change of state**: there was something before, now there isn't. We'll cover it in Unit 10.
**[还|hái] = still, else.** [你还有别的吗|Nǐ hái yǒu bié de ma]？ = anything else?

grammars.title: Colors and qualities
after: Color words are almost always followed by 色 (*sè*, “color”) when they stand alone, but 色 is dropped when the color attaches directly to a noun: [红色|hóngsè] red → [红车|hóng chē] red car.

blocks.text: Words for things stick fastest when the things are right in front of you. After reading the table, close the book for a moment, look around, and name ten things you see using [这是…|Zhè shì…].

blocks.title: 东西 — a lifesaver word
items: **[东西|dōngxi]** literally means “east west”, but it means “thing, stuff”. Use it for anything whose name you don't know.
[这是什么东西|Zhè shì shénme dōngxi]？ — “what is this thing?”
[我要买点儿东西|Wǒ yào mǎi diǎnr dōngxi]。 — “I want to buy some stuff.”
⚠️ Never use it for **people**. [他不是东西|Tā bú shì dōngxi] is a fairly harsh insult, not “he isn't a thing”.

sections.title: Asking about things when you don't know the word

blocks.text: You'll often be in this situation: you see something, don't know its name, and want to find out. These sentences are enough for your whole first year.

head: Sentence
When to use it
rows: [这个用中文怎么说|Zhège yòng Zhōngwén zěnme shuō]？
“How do you say this in Chinese?”
[这个字怎么念|Zhège zì zěnme niàn]？
[请再说一遍|Qǐng zài shuō yí biàn]。
“Please say that again.” The most useful sentence of your first week
[请说慢一点儿|Qǐng shuō màn yìdiǎnr]。
“I don't understand.” More honest than nodding along

blocks.title: Three emergency sentences to learn today
items: **[请再说一遍|Qǐng zài shuō yí biàn]。** — Please say that again.
**[我不明白|Wǒ bù míngbai]。** — I don't understand.
**[这个用中文怎么说|Zhège yòng Zhōngwén zěnme shuō]？** — How do you say this in Chinese?
These three keep a conversation from dying in the tenth second. Learn them now, not later — you'll use them more often than all the vocabulary in this unit combined.
